title: Getting ready to listen
subtitle: Context, spelling and numbers
summary: Use the introduction to each section to predict the context, then write names and numbers exactly as you hear them.

lesson.heading: The context is spoken, not printed
lesson.text: Before each section you hear an introduction telling you **who** is speaking, **what** they are talking about and **why**. That is the context, and it is not written on the question paper. You also get 30-45 seconds to read the questions - use it to predict what you are about to hear.

examples.text: *You will hear a woman asking a travel agent about skiing trips.*
examples.note: Context: organising travel - expect dates, prices and destinations.

examples.text: *You will hear a student telling other students about a research project.*
examples.note: Context: describing a research project - expect aims and methods.

lesson.note: You hear the recording **only once**, so a prediction you made in advance is worth more than perfect concentration on the day.

lesson.heading: What each section sounds like
rows: An everyday conversation - booking, enquiring, arranging
A monologue on a general topic - a tour, a radio talk
An academic conversation - students and a tutor
lesson.note: The sections get harder as you go. Knowing how many voices to expect helps you follow who is answering.

lesson.heading: Spelling is marked
lesson.text: In Section 1 you often have to write a name that is spelt out for you, and you hear it **only once**. A misspelt answer is marked wrong even when you clearly heard the word, so practise the English alphabet until the letters come without thinking.

examples.text: *Is that **spelt the same as** the colour?* - *Yes, but **with an E at the end**.*
*That's right, **all one word and all** lower case.*
*It's just **three letters and three numbers**. It's HLP 528.*
examples.note: A registration number, not a name.

lesson.note: Speakers rarely spell letter by letter. Listen for the trick they use instead - a comparison, a well-known word, or a count of letters.

lesson.heading: The pairs that cost marks
lesson.note: Say both out loud. The difference you can produce is the difference you can hear.

lesson.heading: You will hear more than one number
lesson.text: The recording almost always contains a number you do not want. It is usually there for a reason the speaker states - an old price, a different customer, another date - so listen past the number to the phrase around it.

examples.note: £80 was the amount she paid *last time*; £105 is the *full* price.
$10 is what *regular* students pay; $5 is an extra fee for equipment.
14th July was the first available date; 1st August is her father's birthday.

lesson.text: Write what you hear in the gap immediately, even if you are not sure. There are 10 extra minutes at the end to copy answers onto the answer sheet - that is the moment to tidy spelling, not now.

exercises.prompt: You hear: *You will hear a conversation between a student and a lecturer about an assignment.* Which Listening section is this most likely to be?
exercises.explanation: Section 3 is a conversation between two or three people in an academic context. Section 1 is an everyday conversation; Sections 2 and 4 are monologues.

exercises.statement: If you miss an answer, you can listen to that part of the recording again.
exercises.explanation: You hear the recording only once. That is why the 30-45 seconds of reading time before each section matters so much - predict, then listen.

exercises.prompt: *Is that spelt the same as the colour?* - *Yes, but with an E at the end.* The name is ___.
exercises.explanation: The speaker does not spell the name out; she compares it to a word you already know and then adds the difference.

exercises.prompt: Sort what you hear into the number you should write down.
A woman is booking a room. Match each number you hear with the reason it is *not* the answer.

pairs.right: the amount she paid last time
the full price, before her discount
an extra fee charged for equipment
her father's birthday, not the party

exercises.prompt: The question is *Registration number:* and you hear *It's just three letters and three numbers. It's HLP 528.* What do you write?
exercises.explanation: Write the registration itself. The phrase *three letters and three numbers* only tells you what shape the answer takes.

exercises.prompt: Build the introduction that tells you a Section 2 monologue is coming.
exercises.answer: You will hear a radio presenter talking about a local festival.
exercises.explanation: One speaker on a general topic - that is Section 2.

exercises.statement: A correct answer that is spelt wrongly still gets the mark.
exercises.explanation: Spelling mistakes are marked wrong in the Listening paper, so check names and spelt-out words when you transfer your answers.

exercises.prompt: In the exam you get ___ seconds to read the questions before each section begins.
exercises.explanation: Use that time to underline key words and predict the kind of answer each gap needs.

exercises.prompt: Why is it useful to know that Section 4 is a monologue?
options: Because the answers are always numbers
Because you will not have to decide which of two speakers gave the answer
Because you are allowed to write two answers
exercises.explanation: With one voice, every answer comes from that voice. In Sections 1 and 3 you sometimes have to notice which speaker said it.
